This is a concise Bash script that computes zeros of the Riemann zeta function using PARI/GP (gp), a computer algebra system specialized in number theory.

What it does, step by step:

  1. Prompts the user for two inputs:

    • n — the upper bound for the imaginary part of the zeros to find (e.g., 30 finds all zeros with imaginary part up to 30)
    • p — decimal precision (number of significant digits)

  2. Invokes PARI/GP in quiet mode (gp -q) via a heredoc, passing those variables in:

    • \p $p — sets the working precision
    • lfuncreate(1) — creates an L-function object representing the Riemann zeta function ζ(s)
    • lfunzeros(L, $n) — computes the zeros on the critical line (Re(s) = ½) up to imaginary part $n

Example usage:

Enter n :       50
Enter precision :  20

Would output the imaginary parts of all non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) up to height 50, like 14.134725..., 21.022039..., etc. — all of which lie on the critical line (consistent with the Riemann Hypothesis).

Requirement: PARI/GP must be installed (sudo apt install pari-gp on Debian/Ubuntu).

Fixed. The root cause was that PARI/GP's for loop only accepts a single expression as its body — multiple semicolon-separated statements must be wrapped in { }. The corrected loop:

for(i=1, #v, {
    print(i, "a: 0.5 + ", v[i], "*I");
    print(i, "b: 0.5 - ", v[i], "*I")
})

Without the braces, GP parsed the second print as a separate top-level statement (outside the loop), and the stray ) at the end caused the cascade of syntax errors you saw.

Riemann Zeta Zero Generator

A lightweight Bash script wrapper for Pari/GP that calculates and displays the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ((\zeta(s))) within a user-defined height range ([n1, n2]) on the critical line ((\text{Re}(s) = 1/2)).

Because non-trivial zeros always appear in complex conjugate pairs due to the symmetry of the zeta function ((\zeta(\bar{s}) = \overline{\zeta(s)})), the output formats them efficiently using 0.5 +/- t*I notation.

Prerequisites

This script requires Pari/GP (a specialized computer algebra system for number theory) installed on your system.

Installation

  • Ubuntu / Debian:
    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install pari-gp
  • macOS (via Homebrew):
    brew install pari
  • Fedora / RHEL:
    sudo dnf install pari-gp

Usage

  1. Save the script as zeta_zeros.sh.
  2. Make it executable:
    chmod +x zeta_zeros.sh
  3. Run the script:
    ./zeta_zeros.sh

Example Input/Output

This program generates the zeros of the Riemann zeta function between n1 and n2.

 Enter n1 : 10
 Enter n2 : 30
 Enter precision : 38

1: 0.5 +/- 14.134725141734693790457251983562470271*I
2: 0.5 +/- 21.022039638771554992628479521231581483*I
3: 0.5 +/- 25.010857580145688763213790992562821819*I

How It Works

  1. Input Validation: Ensures that the inputs for the lower bound (n1), upper bound (n2), and real decimal precision (p) are strictly positive integers, and that $n1 \le n2$.
  2. Computational Engine: Passes the parameters directly to an interactive gp quiet shell session (gp -q).
  3. L-Function Evaluation: Uses Pari/GP's highly optimized lfuncreate(1) and lfunzeros() built-ins to compute the imaginary parts of the zeros via explicit formulas and rigorous numerical tracking.

That's a well-written README — clear, mathematically precise, and covers installation across all major platforms. A few minor suggestions if you'd like to refine it further:

  1. \(\zeta(s)\) / \(\text{Re}(s)\) rendering — the LaTeX delimiters only render on platforms that support MathJax/KaTeX (e.g. GitHub doesn't render inline \(...\) by default; it uses $...$). If this is destined for GitHub, swap to $\zeta(s)$ style.

  2. Step 1 of Usage — the script is currently named riemann_zeros.sh, so either the README or the script should be renamed to match. Worth making explicit.

  3. Precision note — it might be worth clarifying that p sets the number of significant decimal digits, and that values below ~15 may give unreliable results for higher zeros.

  4. Range semantics — n1 and n2 are heights on the imaginary axis, not zero indices. The example (n1=10, n2=30) makes this clear implicitly, but a one-liner like "e.g. entering 10 and 100 finds all zeros with imaginary part between 10 and 100" would help first-time users.

Otherwise it's solid — the conjugate pair explanation with the symmetry equation ζ(s̄) = ζ(s)‾ is a nice touch. Are you planning to host this on GitHub? I can help add a badge, license section, or tweak the LaTeX delimiters accordingly.

#!/bin/bash

Riemann Zeta Zero Generator

if ! command -v gp &> /dev/null; then echo "Error: Pari/GP not installed." exit 1 fi

Accept arguments or prompt

n1=${1:-$(read -p "Enter n1 : " val; echo $val)} n2=${2:-$(read -p "Enter n2 : " val; echo $val)} p=${3:-$(read -p "Enter precision : " val; echo $val)}

Validate

if ! [[ "$n1" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$n2" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$p" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then echo "Error: Inputs must be positive integers." exit 1 fi if (( n1 > n2 )); then echo "Error: n1 must be <= n2." exit 1 fi

Run Pari/GP

gp -q <<EOF \p $p L = lfuncreate(1); v = lfunzeros(L, [$n1, $n2]); for(i=1, #v, printf("%3d: 0.5 +/- %s*I\n", i, v[i])) EOF

Nice upgrade. Here's a quick breakdown of what changed:

gp availability check — the new command -v gp guard fails fast with a clean error before any input is collected, rather than running the whole script only to crash at the heredoc.

Dual input mode — ${1:-$(read -p ... )} is clever: positional args take priority, falling back to interactive prompts. This makes the script both scriptable (./zeta_zeros.sh 10 100 38) and user-friendly when run bare.

Consolidated validation — the three regex checks are merged into a single && expression, tidier than three separate || blocks.

printf instead of print — the switch to printf("%3d: 0.5 +/- %s*I\n", i, v[i]) gives right-aligned zero indices (up to 3 digits), which keeps columns neat for larger ranges. One thing to verify: PARI/GP's printf uses %s to stringify t_REAL values, so the precision set by \p should still flow through correctly into v[i]'s string representation.

One potential edge case worth testing: the ${1:-$(read -p ...)} fallback uses a subshell, so on some shells the prompt may not display if stdin isn't a terminal. Wrapping those in a helper function or using an explicit if [ -z "$1" ] branch would be more portable. Want me to make that adjustment?

    ├── B.py → bernoulli.py   (Bernoulli numbers via fractions)
    └── E.py → zigzag.py      (Euler/zigzag numbers via DP)

What each module does:

  • bernoulli.py — generates Bernoulli numbers lazily as exact Fractions using the iterative triangle algorithm. The standalone run prints B(0)–B(60).

  • B.py — thin wrapper: B(n) pulls the n-th Bernoulli number from the generator.

  • zigzag.py — computes zigzag (tangent/secant) numbers via a DP table. zigzag(n, k) fills an (n+1)×(k+1) grid; the diagonal entry gives the n-th zigzag number (also called Euler zigzag numbers / up/down numbers).

  • E.py — thin wrapper: E(n) = zigzag(n, n), returning the n-th Euler number.

  • zeta.py — the core. Computes ζ(n) exactly:

    • Positive even n: uses the Basel-type formula involving Bernoulli numbers: (-1)^(n/2+1) · B(n) · 2^(n-1) / n! · πⁿ
    • Positive odd n: falls into the error branch (closed forms unknown), but returns a tangent-number-based expression involving Euler numbers
    • Non-positive n: uses (-1)^(-n) · B(1-n) / (1-n) (the trivial zeros / negative integer values)
    • Output is a zeta object with .z (the rational coefficient) and .s (the π superscript string)

  • piprime.py — uses the Euler product formula for ζ(n): ζ(n) = ∏(1 - p⁻ⁿ)⁻¹ over primes p, rearranged to extract π: π = (∏(1 - p⁻ⁿ) · ζ(n))^(-1/n)

A few things worth noting:

  1. The odd-n branch in zeta.py silently proceeds after printing the error — it returns an Euler-number expression rather than raising an exception, which could confuse callers like piprime.py.

  2. piprime.py depends on nextPrime.NP which isn't in the uploads — is that a file you have locally?

  3. zigzag.py has inconsistent blank lines (every line double-spaced) — likely a formatting artifact.

The missing piece. The full library is now complete:

prime.py — isPrime(n, r, i, c)

A hybrid primality test with two layers:

  • Fast path: delegates to Crypto.Util.number.isPrime (a Miller-Rabin implementation) when c=True
  • Trial division fallback (when r=True): walks divisors using a 6k±1 wheel — skips multiples of 2 and 3, stepping i by +2/+4 alternately via (i-3)%6. Returns the smallest factor if composite, True if prime.
  • The isDivisible lambda is doing double duty: returns n (truthy, ≠ factor) if not divisible, or i (the factor) if divisible — then if d - n detects the factor case.

nextPrime.py — NP(n)

Finds the next prime after n, also using the 6k±1 wheel:

  • Special-cases n=2→3 and n=3→5 directly
  • Otherwise snaps to the next candidate on the 6k±1 grid with n + (n-3)%6, then steps by (m-3)%6 (+2 or +4 alternately) until isPrime passes

The full dependency graph is now:

piprime.py
├── nextPrime.py → prime.py → Crypto.Util.number
└── zeta.py
    ├── B.py → bernoulli.py
    └── E.py → zigzag.py

This is a PARI/GP implementation of Gilbreath's conjecture — a beautiful unsolved problem in number theory. Here's a breakdown:

What it does:

  1. Takes n — the number of primes to start with
  2. Row 0 is the first n primes: [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ...]
  3. Each subsequent row takes absolute differences of consecutive elements: |a[i+1] - a[i]|
  4. Checks that every row (after row 0) starts with 1 — which is exactly what Gilbreath's conjecture asserts

Example for n=6:

Row 0: [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]
Row 1: [1, 2, 2, 4, 2]
Row 2: [1, 0, 2, 2]
Row 3: [1, 2, 0]
Row 4: [1, 2]
Row 5: [1]

Every row begins with 1 — the conjecture holds (as it has for all verified cases).

A few observations on the code:

  • prime(i) in PARI/GP returns the i-th prime directly — clean and efficient
  • vector(#row - 1, i, abs(row[i] - row[i+1])) is idiomatic GP for the difference step
  • The break on failure is correct but PARI/GP's break() requires parentheses — break alone may not work in all GP versions; worth changing to break()
  • The conjecture has been verified for millions of primes but remains unproven — this is a nice empirical explorer

Is this going into the number theory library alongside the zeta/Bernoulli modules, or is it a standalone GP script?

                     );

A few things to flag here:

read -P is fish shell syntax — the flag for displaying a prompt in fish. In bash it's read -p (lowercase). If this is intentional for fish, that's fine, but it won't work in #!/bin/bash.

The echo "..." | gp -q approach works but has one gotcha: the entire GP block is a single shell string with escaped quotes throughout, which gets fragile. The heredoc pattern you used in riemann_zeros.sh is cleaner and avoids all the \" escaping:

gp -q <<EOF
my(n = $n);
if(type(n) != "t_INT" || n < 1,
    error("Input must be a positive integer.")
);
...
EOF

Input validation — unlike riemann_zeros.sh, there's no bash-level integer check before passing $n to GP. If the user enters a string, GP's type() check catches it, but the error message will be a GP error rather than your clean bash message. Worth adding:

if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "Error: Input must be a positive integer."
    exit 1
fi

break vs break() — same issue flagged earlier; worth confirming which GP version you're targeting.

import open3d as o3d import numpy as np

Define prime colors (R, G, B normalized between 0 and 1)

PRIME_COLORS = { 2: [0.9, 0.1, 0.1], # Red 3: [0.1, 0.3, 0.9], # Blue 5: [0.1, 0.7, 0.2], # Green 7: [0.9, 0.8, 0.1], # Yellow 11: [0.9, 0.5, 0.1], # Orange 13: [0.6, 0.1, 0.8] # Purple } DEFAULT_COLOR = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] # Gray for any primes higher than 13

def get_prime_factors(n): """Returns a list of prime factors for a given number.""" factors = [] d = 2 while d * d <= n: while (n % d) == 0: factors.append(d) n //= d d += 1 if n > 1: factors.append(n) return sorted(factors)

def create_floor(x, y, z, color, size=1.0, height=0.5): """Creates a single 3D block (floor) at the specified grid coordinate.""" mesh = o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh.create_box(width=size0.9, height=height0.9, depth=size*0.9) mesh.compute_vertex_normals()

# Position the floor in 3D space
translation = np.array([x * size, z * height, y * size])
mesh.translate(translation)
mesh.paint_uniform_color(color)
return mesh

def build_factor_city(numbers_grid): """Generates the 3D scene based on a 2D layout layout of numbers.""" scene_geometries = []

for row_idx, row in enumerate(numbers_grid):
    for col_idx, number in enumerate(row):
        if number <= 1:
            continue # Skip 0 or 1 as they cannot be constructed from prime floors
            
        factors = get_prime_factors(number)
        
        # Stack the factors on top of each other to create the building
        for floor_level, prime in enumerate(factors):
            color = PRIME_COLORS.get(prime, DEFAULT_COLOR)
            floor_mesh = create_floor(col_idx, row_idx, floor_level, color)
            scene_geometries.append(floor_mesh)
            
return scene_geometries

if name == "main": # Define a custom grid layout for your Factor City # Each item represents the composite number of the building at that coordinate city_grid = [, , , [2, 3, 5, 7] # Single-story prime baseline ]

print("Generating Factor City meshes...")
geometries = build_factor_city(city_grid)

# Create the visualization window
vis = o3d.visualization.Visualizer()
vis.create_window(window_name="Factor City Interactive Explorer", width=1280, height=720)

for geom in geometries:
    vis.add_geometry(geom)
    
# Configure rendering options for clean visualization
opt = vis.get_render_option()
opt.background_color = np.array([0.9, 0.95, 1.0]) # Soft sky blue sky
opt.show_coordinate_frame = False

print("\nControls:")
print("  - Left-Click & Drag: Rotate City")
print("  - Shift + Right-Click & Drag: Move/Pan Map")
print("  - Mouse Scroll Wheel: Zoom In/Out")

vis.run()
vis.destroy_window()

This is a fun concept — a 3D "city" where each building's floors are stacked prime factors, colored by prime. A few things to note:

Bug: city_grid is broken

city_grid = [,
 ,
 ,
    [2, 3, 5, 7]
]

The first three rows are empty/missing — likely placeholders you haven't filled in yet. This will cause a SyntaxError. You probably want something like:

city_grid = [
    [12, 18, 30, 42],   # Row 0 — composite buildings
    [6,  10, 15, 21],   # Row 1
    [4,  9,  25, 49],   # Row 2 — prime squares
    [2,  3,  5,  7]     # Row 3 — single-story prime baseline
]

Design observations:

  • get_prime_factors returns factors with repetition (e.g. 12 → [2, 2, 3]), so buildings stack one floor per prime factor including multiplicity — that's a nice touch, 12 is 3 floors tall.
  • The 0.9 scaling on box dimensions (size*0.9, height*0.9) creates a small gap between blocks — good for visual separation.
  • z * height as the Y axis in Open3D is correct since O3D uses Y-up coordinates.
  • Numbers ≤ 1 are skipped, so 1 leaves an empty lot and 0 is ignored — reasonable.

Minor issues:

  • "Soft sky blue sky" — double "sky" in the comment
  • No camera positioning — the default view may not be ideal for a grid; worth setting an initial viewpoint with vis.get_view_control().set_front(...)
  • Primes > 13 all share gray — buildings with large prime factors (e.g. 17, 19) will look identical at that floor

import open3d as o3d
import open3d.visualization.gui as gui
import open3d.visualization.rendering as rendering
import numpy as np

# Use your existing setup variables, PRIME_COLORS, and get_prime_factors function here...

def build_factor_city_with_labels(grid, scene):
    """Builds the city and adds text labels above each rooftop."""
    mat = rendering.MaterialRecord()
    mat.shader = "defaultLit"

    for row_idx, row in enumerate(grid):
        for col_idx, number in enumerate(row):
            if number <= 1:
                continue
            
            factors = get_prime_factors(number)
            
            # Place the physical blocks
            for level, prime in enumerate(factors):
                color = PRIME_COLORS.get(prime, DEFAULT_COLOR)
                block = create_block(col_idx, row_idx, level, color)
                scene.add_geometry(f"block_{row_idx}_{col_idx}_{level}", block, mat)
            
            # Calculate text placement (just above the top floor)
            top_y = len(factors) * BLOCK_HEIGHT + 0.2
            center_x = col_idx * BLOCK_SIZE + (BLOCK_SIZE / 2)
            center_z = row_idx * BLOCK_SIZE + (BLOCK_SIZE / 2)
            
            # Format math string: e.g., "12 = 2 × 2 × 3"
            factor_str = " × ".join(map(str, factors))
            label_text = f"{number} = {factor_str}"
            
            # Generate a 3D label anchor point
            scene.add_3d_label(np.array([center_x, top_y, center_z]), label_text)

# Execution using modern UI window instead of legacy Visualizer
if __name__ == "__main__":
    gui.Application.instance.initialize()
    window = gui.Application.instance.create_window("Factor City - Modern View", 1280, 720)
    scene_widget = gui.SceneWidget()
    scene_widget.scene = rendering.Open3DScene(window.renderer)
    scene_widget.scene.set_background_color(np.array([0.08, 0.08, 0.12, 1.0]))
    
    # Build City & Text Elements
    build_factor_city_with_labels(CITY_GRID, scene_widget.scene)
    
    # Setup Camera Bounds
    bounds = scene_widget.scene.bounding_box
    scene_widget.setup_camera(60, bounds, bounds.get_center())
    window.add_child(scene_widget)
    
    gui.Application.instance.run()

# Insert this animation logic right before vis.run() in your original file:

# 1. Create a "delivery truck" block
truck = o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh.create_sphere(radius=0.15)
truck.paint_uniform_color([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) # White sphere factor delivery
vis.add_geometry(truck)

# 2. State variables for animation pathing
state = {"time": 0.0}

def move_delivery_truck(visualizer):
    state["time"] += 0.02
    
    # Make the ball bounce/travel along the street grid smoothly
    new_x = 1.5 + np.sin(state["time"]) * 1.5
    new_z = 2.0 + np.cos(state["time"]) * 2.0
    new_y = 0.1 + abs(np.sin(state["time"] * 3)) * 0.3 # Hopping animation
    
    # Reset translation matrix cleanly each frame
    truck.translate(np.array([new_x, new_y, new_z]), relative=False)
    
    # Update geometry changes on screen
    visualizer.update_geometry(truck)
    return True

# 3. Tell Open3D to call this math logic on every screen refresh frame
vis.register_animation_callback(move_delivery_truck)
vis.run()

Both features are fully integrated. Here's how everything fits together:

Two runtime modes, selected via CLI flag:

python factor_city.py           # --labels (default) — modern GUI with equations
python factor_city.py --animate # legacy Visualizer with truck animation

--labels mode uses gui.Application + rendering.Open3DScene:

  • Every building gets a floating add_3d_label showing e.g. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3
  • Legend cubes also get p=2, p=3... labels beside them
  • 4-channel background color (RGBA) required by this API — that's why it differs from the legacy path

--animate mode uses the legacy Visualizer:

  • The delivery truck sphere bounces along a sinusoidal street path scaled to the actual grid dimensions (rather than hardcoded 1.5 / 2.0 offsets that could send it off-city)
  • register_animation_callback returning True keeps the loop alive

Key integration decision: the two APIs (Visualizer vs gui.Application) are incompatible in the same process, so they're cleanly separated into run_with_animation() and run_with_labels() rather than trying to merge them — which would crash at runtime.

import sys
import open3d as o3d
import open3d.visualization.gui as gui
import open3d.visualization.rendering as rendering
import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prime color palette (RGB, normalized 0–1)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRIME_COLORS = {
    2:  [0.90, 0.10, 0.10],   # Red
    3:  [0.10, 0.30, 0.90],   # Blue
    5:  [0.10, 0.70, 0.20],   # Green
    7:  [0.90, 0.80, 0.10],   # Yellow
    11: [0.90, 0.50, 0.10],   # Orange
    13: [0.60, 0.10, 0.80],   # Purple
    17: [0.10, 0.80, 0.85],   # Cyan
    19: [0.85, 0.10, 0.60],   # Magenta
    23: [0.40, 0.80, 0.40],   # Lime
    29: [0.80, 0.40, 0.20],   # Sienna
    31: [0.20, 0.40, 0.80],   # Steel blue
}
DEFAULT_COLOR = [0.55, 0.55, 0.55]   # Gray — primes > 31

BLOCK_SIZE   = 1.0
BLOCK_HEIGHT = 0.5
GAP          = 0.1

CITY_GRID = [,    # 2·3·5 / 2·3·7 / 2·3·11 / 2·3·13,    # 2²·3  / 2·3²  / 2²·5   / 2²·7,    # 2³    / 3³    / 5²      / 7²,    # 2·3   / 2·5   / 3·5     / 5·7,     # single-floor prime baseline
]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def get_prime_factors(n: int) -> list[int]:
    factors = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        factors.append(n)
    return factors

def create_block(col: int, row: int, level: int, color: list) -> o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh:
    w = BLOCK_SIZE   * (1 - GAP)
    h = BLOCK_HEIGHT * (1 - GAP)
    d = BLOCK_SIZE   * (1 - GAP)

    mesh = o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh.create_box(width=w, height=h, depth=d)
    mesh.compute_vertex_normals()

    offset_x = col   * BLOCK_SIZE   + GAP / 2
    offset_y = level * BLOCK_HEIGHT + GAP / 2
    offset_z = row   * BLOCK_SIZE   + GAP / 2
    mesh.translate(np.array([offset_x, offset_y, offset_z]))
    mesh.paint_uniform_color(color)
    return mesh

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Modern GUI App Class (Supports dynamic animation frames & UI labels)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
class FactorCityApp:

import sys
import open3d as o3d
import open3d.visualization.gui as gui
import open3d.visualization.rendering as rendering
import numpy as np

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prime color palette (RGB, normalized 0–1)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
PRIME_COLORS = {
    2:  [0.90, 0.10, 0.10],   # Red
    3:  [0.10, 0.30, 0.90],   # Blue
    5:  [0.10, 0.70, 0.20],   # Green
    7:  [0.90, 0.80, 0.10],   # Yellow
    11: [0.90, 0.50, 0.10],   # Orange
    13: [0.60, 0.10, 0.80],   # Purple
    17: [0.10, 0.80, 0.85],   # Cyan
    19: [0.85, 0.10, 0.60],   # Magenta
    23: [0.40, 0.80, 0.40],   # Lime
    29: [0.80, 0.40, 0.20],   # Sienna
    31: [0.20, 0.40, 0.80],   # Steel blue
}
DEFAULT_COLOR = [0.55, 0.55, 0.55]   # Gray — primes > 31

BLOCK_SIZE   = 1.0
BLOCK_HEIGHT = 0.5
GAP          = 0.1

INITIAL_GRID = [,    # 2·3·5 / 2·3·7 / 2·3·11 / 2·3·13,    # 2²·3  / 2·3²  / 2²·5   / 2²·7,    # 2³    / 3³    / 5²      / 7²,    # 2·3   / 2·5   / 3·5     / 5·7,     # single-floor prime baseline
]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def get_prime_factors(n: int) -> list[int]:
    factors = []
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        factors.append(n)
    return factors

def create_block(col: int, row: int, level: int, color: list) -> o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh:
    w = BLOCK_SIZE   * (1 - GAP)
    h = BLOCK_HEIGHT * (1 - GAP)
    d = BLOCK_SIZE   * (1 - GAP)
    mesh = o3d.geometry.TriangleMesh.create_box(width=w, height=h, depth=d)
    mesh.compute_vertex_normals()
    offset_x = col   * BLOCK_SIZE   + GAP / 2
    offset_y = level * BLOCK_HEIGHT + GAP / 2
    offset_z = row   * BLOCK_SIZE   + GAP / 2
    mesh.translate(np.array([offset_x, offset_y, offset_z]))
    mesh.paint_uniform_color(color)
    return mesh

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dynamic Factor City Application
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

        self.window = gui.Application.instance.create_window(
            "Factor City Lab — Ultimate Prime Explorer", 1400, 800
        )
        
        # Main Rendering Window
        self.scene_widget = gui.SceneWidget()
        self.scene_widget.scene = rendering.Open3D

Gist or repo?

For this project I'd go with a repo — here's why:

It's grown well beyond a single file. You now have a natural multi-file structure:

factor-city/
├── factor_city.py
├── README.md
├── number_theory/
│   ├── prime.py
│   ├── nextPrime.py
│   ├── bernoulli.py
│   ├── B.py
│   ├── zigzag.py
│   ├── E.py
│   ├── zeta.py
│   └── piprime.py
└── requirements.txt

A repo gives you issue tracking, a proper README rendered on the landing page, release tags, and room to grow (e.g. a Gilbreath script, more visualizers). A Gist is fine for the shell scripts (riemann_zeros.sh, gilbreath.sh) since those are genuinely self-contained single files.

So the split would be:

  • Repo → factor-city (Python visualizer + number theory library)
  • Gists → riemann_zeros.sh, gilbreath.sh

Want help writing a requirements.txt, a top-level __init__.py for the library, or a repo description/topics for GitHub?

number_theory is completely different

You're right — number_theory is its own independent library (Bernoulli numbers, zeta values, Euler/zigzag numbers, prime tools), while factor_city.py just happens to use prime factorization internally via its own self-contained get_prime_factors function. They don't share any code.

So the split would be:

  • Repo 1 → factor-city — just factor_city.py + README.md + requirements.txt
  • Repo 2 → number-theory — the Python library (prime.py, nextPrime.py, bernoulli.py, B.py, zigzag.py, E.py, zeta.py, piprime.py) with its own README
  • Gists → riemann_zeros.sh, gilbreath.sh

Licence?

For a math/visualization project like this, the two most common choices:

MIT — if you want maximum permissiveness. Anyone can use, modify, and distribute with minimal restriction. Best if you want the code to be widely usable.

GPL-3.0 — if you want any derivative work to also be open source. Stronger copyleft.

Given that this is a personal creative/educational project and Open3D itself is MIT licensed, MIT is the natural fit — keeps things simple and consistent with the dependency.

Initial commit: Factor City 3D prime factorization visualizer

v1.0.0

Release notes:

v1.0.0 — Initial Release

Factor City is an interactive 3D prime factorization visualizer built with Open3D. Each integer in a configurable grid is rendered as a tower of colored blocks, one floor per prime factor, where each prime has a distinct color.

Features

  • 3D block towers encoding prime factorization of each number in the city grid
  • 11-prime color palette (primes 2–31), gray fallback for larger primes
  • Floating equation labels above each rooftop (n = p₁ × p₂ × …)
  • Animated delivery truck orbiting the city with hopping motion
  • Building inspector — click any tower to see its full factorization in the side panel
  • Selected building highlight via color brightening
  • Custom tower deployment — enter any integer ≥ 2 and place it in the grid at runtime
  • Speed slider, animation toggle, and label toggle via side control panel
  • Color-coded prime legend rendered in the 3D scene

Requirements

  • Python 3.10+
  • open3d ≥ 0.18.0
  • numpy ≥ 1.26.0

AABB (0,0) t=inf AABB (0,1) t=inf AABB (0,2) t=inf AABB (0,3) t=inf AABB (1,0) t=inf AABB (1,1) t=inf AABB (1,2) t=inf AABB (1,3) t=inf AABB (2,0) t=inf AABB (2,1) t=inf AABB (2,2) t=inf AABB (2,3) t=inf AABB (3,0) t=inf AABB (3,1) t=inf AABB (3,2) t=inf AABB (3,3) t=inf AABB (4,0) t=inf AABB (4,1) t=inf AABB (4,2) t=inf AABB (4,3) t=inf best_hit=None best_t=inf

All t=inf means the ray is missing every AABB. Need to see the actual ray coordinates — can you paste the [PICK] line that appears above those AABB lines?

[PICK] vp=(330,437) near=[ 2.58 0.65 11.24] far=[-inf -inf -inf] |ray|=inf

far=[-inf -inf -inf] is the problem — camera.unproject() with depth=1.0 returns infinity in this Open3D build, making the ray direction undefined. The fix is to use a small offset instead of 1.0 for the far point:

Replace depth=1.0 far point with depth=0.01 mid point
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"Done\n","stderr":""}
Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

The depth parameter in camera.unproject() maps to NDC depth, and 1.0 (far plane) overflows to infinity in this build's projection. Using 0.01 instead gives a second point just slightly in front of the near plane, which is enough to establish a direction for the ray — the ray is then extended infinitely via the AABB intersection math anyway.

Run it again and paste the [PICK] line — mid should now have finite coordinates and the AABBs should start returning real t values.

Now it's working: [PICK] vp=(316,439) near=[ 2.58 0.65 11.24] mid=[ 2.58 0.65 11.23] |ray|=0.0011

Fix building inspector, Q-to-quit, and Open3D API compatibility on Windows

A few things to address here:

read -P → read -p — still fish syntax, won't work in bash.

primes(n) — good upgrade from vector(n, i, prime(i)), cleaner PARI/GP built-in.

break → break() — PARI/GP requires parentheses.

Formatting — the inline semicolons and collapsed whitespace make it hard to read and maintain. The heredoc pattern from riemann_zeros.sh solves all of this cleanly.

#!/bin/bash

Title: Gilbreath Triangle Generator

Description: Generates a Gilbreath Triangle for the first n primes

and verifies Gilbreath's conjecture at each row.

Dependencies: pari-gp (Computer Algebra System)

Check for Pari/GP

if ! command -v gp &> /dev/null; then echo "Error: Pari/GP is not installed. See README for install instructions." exit 1 fi

printf "This program generates a Gilbreath Triangle.\n\n"

Accept arguments or prompt

n=${1:-$(read -p "Enter the number of primes (n): " val; echo $val)} quiet=${2:-0}

Validate input

if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || (( n < 1 )); then echo "Error: Input must be a positive integer." exit 1 fi

if ! [[ "$quiet" =~ ^[01]$ ]]; then echo "Error: Second argument must be 0 or 1 for quiet mode." exit 1 fi

Run Pari/GP

gp -q << GPEOF my(n = $n); my(quiet = $quiet); my(row = vector(n,i,prime(i))); if(!quiet, print("Row 0: ", row)); my(failed=0, t=gettime());

for(r = 1, n - 1, row = vector(#row - 1, i, abs(row[i] - row[i+1])); if(!quiet, print("Row ", r, ": ", row));

if(row[1]!= 1,
    print("Gilbreath condition failed at row ", r);
    failed=1;
    break()
)

); if(!failed, print("Gilbreath holds for first ", n, " primes")); printf("Time: %.3f s\n", gettime()/1000); GPEOF

Clean upgrade. A few observations:

Good additions:

  • quiet mode — useful for large n where printing every row is slow; lets you benchmark pure computation time
  • failed flag — clean way to print the success message only if no row broke the conjecture
  • gettime() timing — nice for empirical performance measurement; gettime() in PARI/GP returns milliseconds since last call, so /1000 correctly gives seconds
  • Error message on missing gp now points to the README

One thing to verify: vector(n,i,prime(i)) vs primes(n) — both work, but primes(n) is a PARI/GP built-in that returns the first n primes directly and is slightly faster. Since you already had it in the previous version, worth keeping:

my(row = primes(n));

Potential edge case: if n = 1, the for(r = 1, 0, ...) loop body never executes (PARI/GP loops don't run when upper bound < lower bound), so it will just print Row 0 and report success — which is technically correct.

The gilbreath.sh error is the same issue we saw before — $n is being treated as a polynomial (t_POL) by PARI/GP, meaning the shell variable isn't expanding inside the heredoc. This happens because the heredoc delimiter GPEOF is unquoted, so $n should expand — but on your Termux/fish setup the read -p subshell isn't passing the value through correctly.

Let me fix it by validating and echoing n explicitly before the heredoc:

The heredoc and $n expansion look correct. The real culprit is the read -p subshell fallback on line 16 — in fish, running the script as bash gilbreath.sh, the subshell $(read -p ... ; echo $val) silently fails and n ends up empty, so PARI/GP sees a literal $n symbol (a polynomial variable) instead of a number. The $(read ... ; echo $val) subshell pattern is the problem — it runs in a child process that has no access to the terminal in some environments, so read gets nothing and n ends up empty. The explicit if/else block reads directly in the current shell, which works reliably everywhere including Termux. Both modes working. Two small things to note:

Time: 0 s — gettime() resets on each call, and for small n the computation is sub-millisecond so it rounds to 0. For large n (e.g. ./gilbreath.sh 10000 1) it will show a meaningful value.

Timing fix — call gettime() once before the loop to start the clock, then once after to read the elapsed time. Currently t = gettime() is set but never used — the final gettime() call measures time since itself (near zero). Small fix if you want accurate timing:

gettime();
for(r = 1, n - 1, ...);
print("Time: ", gettime()/1000.0, " s");

v1.0.0 — Initial Release

Scripts

riemann_zeros.sh

  • Computes non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) in a user-defined height range [n1, n2]
  • Configurable decimal precision via PARI/GP's \p
  • Outputs conjugate pairs as 0.5 +/- t*I

  • Argument mode: ./gilbreath.sh n [quiet]
  • Input validation and gp availability check

🔧 Prerequisites

All scripts require PARI/GP (Computer Algebra System specialized in number theory).

💻 Installation

  • Ubuntu / Debian:
    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install pari-gp
  • macOS (via Homebrew):
    brew install pari
  • Fedora / RHEL:
    sudo dnf install pari-gp
  • Windows: Download from pari.math.u-bordeaux.fr (pari.math.u-bordeaux.fr in Bing)

📜 Scripts

riemann_zeros.sh

Computes the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) within a user-defined height range [n1, n2] on the critical line (Re(s) = 1/2).

Usage:

chmod +x riemann_zeros.sh
./riemann_zeros.sh [n1] [n2] [precision]

Example Output:

1: 0.5 +/- 14.134725141734693790457251983562470271*I
2: 0.5 +/- 21.022039638771554992628479593896281302*I
3: 0.5 +/- 25.010857580145688763213790992562821819*I

gilbreath.sh

Generates a Gilbreath Triangle for the first n primes and verifies Gilbreath's conjecture at each row.

Usage:

chmod +x gilbreath.sh
./gilbreath.sh [n] [quiet]

Example Output:

Row 0: [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]
Row 1: [1, 2, 2, 4, 2]
Row 2: [1, 0, 2, 2]
Row 3: [1, 2, 0]
Row 4: [1, 2]
Row 5: [1]
Gilbreath holds for first 6 primes
Time: 0.001 s

⚡ Quick Start

git clone https://github.com/Abhrankan-Chakrabarti/pari-gp-scripts.git
cd pari-gp-scripts
./riemann_zeros.sh 10 30 38
./gilbreath.sh 10000 1

Contributing to PARI/GP Scripts

We welcome contributions to expand this collection of Bash wrappers for PARI/GP and classical problems in number theory.

🛠️ How to Contribute

  1. Fork the repository

    git clone https://github.com/your-username/pari-gp-scripts.git
cd pari-gp-scripts

  2. Create a new branch

    git checkout -b feature/new-script

  3. Add your script

    • Place it in the root directory (e.g., prime_gaps.sh).
    • Follow the conventions below.

  4. Test your script

    • Ensure it runs on Linux/macOS/Windows (if applicable).
    • Validate inputs before passing to gp.
    • Confirm outputs are clear and consistent.

  5. Commit and push

    git add prime_gaps.sh
git commit -m "Add prime gaps explorer script"
git push origin feature/new-script

  6. Open a Pull Request

    • Describe the purpose of your script.
    • Include usage examples and sample output.

📐 Script Conventions

Each script should include:

  • Header block with Title, Description, Dependencies.
  • Check for gp availability:
    if ! command -v gp &> /dev/null; then
    echo "Error: Pari/GP is not installed."
    exit 1
fi
  • Argument mode with interactive fallback:
    n=${1:-$(read -p "Enter n: " val; echo $val)}
  • Input validation before calling GP.
  • Consistent output formatting (aligned rows, clear labels).
  • Timing via gettime() when useful.

🚀 Ideas for New Scripts

  • Prime gap explorer
  • Möbius function table
  • Goldbach partition checker
  • Dirichlet L-function zeros
  • Euler product approximations

✅ Code Style

  • Use Bash 4+ syntax.
  • Keep scripts lightweight and readable.
  • Prefer printf over echo for formatted output.
  • Document usage with examples in the README.

🤝 Community Guidelines

  • Be respectful and constructive in discussions.
  • Keep contributions focused on number theory and PARI/GP.
  • Ensure scripts are original and not copied from copyrighted sources.

This CONTRIBUTING file will make your repo feel like a true collaborative project.

The GP script is correct — my(n = 14) is there. But GP still treats n as a polynomial after that. This means my(n = 14) is being parsed correctly but GP is resetting n back to a polynomial symbol for the subsequent lines — which happens when the input isn't treated as a single session but as separate statements.

The fix is to put everything in a single GP block wrapped in {}:

Wrap GP script in single block to fix my() scoping
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"","stderr":""}
Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

The issue is that my() in PARI/GP creates lexically scoped variables — they only exist within the enclosing block. When the script is piped line by line, each my() declaration is its own top-level statement and the variable goes out of scope immediately. Wrapping everything in { } creates a single block so all my() declarations share the same scope throughout.

This is also why gilbreath.sh works — the for() loop keeps everything inside one GP expression.

Working perfectly in both modes. The my() scoping fix also explains why gilbreath.sh needed the echo "$GP_SCRIPT" approach — the block structure there kept everything in scope via the for() expression.

Also worth updating CONTRIBUTING.md to add this as a third GP convention: always wrap multi-statement GP scripts in { } to preserve my() scoping. Want me to do that and also add prime_gaps.sh to the README?

     1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Title:        Prime Gap Explorer (Optimized)
     3	# Description:  Computes max prime gaps efficiently using continuous streaming.
     4	# Dependencies: pari-gp
     5	
     6	if ! command -v gp &> /dev/null; then
     7	    echo "Error: Pari/GP is not installed."
     8	    exit 1
     9	fi
    10	
    11	printf "This program computes prime gaps for the first n primes.\n\n"
    12	
    13	if [[ -n "$1" ]]; then
    14	    n=$1
    15	else
    16	    printf "Enter the number of primes (n): "
    17	    read n
    18	fi
    19	
    20	if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || (( n < 2 )); then
    21	    echo "Error: Input must be an integer >= 2."
    22	    exit 1
    23	fi
    24	
    25	# Optimized GP script: Uses a simple loop to keep memory usage at virtually zero.
    26	GP_SCRIPT="
    27	{
    28	    my(n = $n, p_prev = 2, p_curr, gap, max_gap = 0);
    29	    gettime();
    30	    
    31	    for(i = 2, n,
    32	        p_curr = prime(i);
    33	        gap = p_curr - p_prev;
    34	        if(gap > max_gap, max_gap = gap);
    35	        p_prev = p_curr;
    36	    );
    37	    
    38	    printf(\"Total Primes Processed: %d\n\", n);
    39	    printf(\"Last Prime Reached:     %d\n\", p_prev);
    40	    printf(\"Max gap found:          %d\n\", max_gap);
    41	    printf(\"Time elapsed:           %.3f s\n\", gettime()/1000.0);
    42	}"
    43	
    44	echo "$GP_SCRIPT" | gp -q
    45	
    46

Nice rewrite. A few observations:

What changed:

  • Dropped the primes and gaps vectors entirely — computes max gap on the fly using p_prev/p_curr, so memory usage is O(1) regardless of n
  • No longer prints every prime and gap — just the summary stats, making it useful for very large n
  • Output is more informative: total primes processed, last prime reached, max gap, and timing

One thing to verify: prime(i) is called n-1 times in a loop, which is O(n log n) — slightly slower than building a primes() vector for small n, but much better for large n where the vector would be expensive to allocate. Good tradeoff.

Minor: the See README for install instructions message was dropped from the gp error — fine since the description says "Optimized" and is leaner overall.

Does this replace the previous prime_gaps.sh in the repo, or live alongside it?

Your call

Replace it — one script per problem is cleaner, and this version is strictly better: lower memory, useful for large n, and the summary output is more informative than printing every gap. No reason to keep the vector version.

Two fixes:

  • \\\\n → \n — inside a double-quoted bash string, \n passes as a literal two-character sequence \n to GP, which GP's printf correctly interprets as a newline

     1	#!/bin/bash
     2	# Title:        Möbius Function Table (True Sieve)
     3	# Description:  Computes μ(n) up to N instantly using an O(N) array sieve.
     4	# Dependencies: pari-gp
     5	
     6	if ! command -v gp &> /dev/null; then
     7	    echo "Error: Pari/GP is not installed. See README for install instructions."
     8	    exit 1
     9	fi
    10	
    11	printf "This program computes the Möbius function μ(n) for integers up to N.\n\n"
    12	
    13	if [[ -n "$1" ]]; then
    14	    N=$1
    15	else
    16	    printf "Enter N (upper bound): "
    17	    read N
    18	fi
    19	
    20	if ! [[ "$N" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || (( N < 1 )); then
    21	    echo "Error: Input must be a positive integer."
    22	    exit 1
    23	fi
    24	
    25	if (( N <= 1000 )); then
    26	    printf "n     μ(n)\n"
    27	    echo "------------"
    28	fi
    29	
    30	# Optimized GP Script: True sieve logic
    31	# 1. Initialize vector with 1s
    32	# 2. Identify prime factors to flip the sign (mu = -mu)
    33	# 3. Identify square prime factors to set mu = 0
    34	GP_SCRIPT="
    35	{
    36	    my(N = $N);
    37	    gettime();
    38	    
    39	    my(mu = vector(N, i, 1));
    40	    
    41	    forprime(p = 2, N,
    42	        \\\\ Flip sign for all multiples of this prime
    43	        forstep(i = p, N, p, mu[i] = -mu[i]);
    44	        
    45	        \\\\ Zero out all multiples of p^2
    46	        my(p2 = p * p);
    47	        if(p2 <= N,
    48	            forstep(j = p2, N, p2, mu[j] = 0)
    49	        );
    50	    );
    51	    
    52	    my(calc_time = gettime() / 1000.0);
    53	    
    54	    if(N <= 1000,
    55	        for(n = 1, N, printf(\"%-5d %d\n\", n, mu[n])),
    56	        printf(\"Skipping full table print for large N (%d values).\n\", N)
    57	    );
    58	    
    59	    printf(\"Calculation Time: %.3f s\n\", calc_time);
    60	}"
    61	
    62	echo "$GP_SCRIPT" | gp -q
    63	
    64

Nice upgrade — a true linear sieve rather than calling moebius(n) per element. The algorithm:

  1. Start with all mu[i] = 1
  2. forprime over all primes p ≤ N — flip sign of every multiple of p (inclusion-exclusion)
  3. Zero out every multiple of p²

This is O(N log log N) — faster than the previous O(N log N) vector approach for large N. The \\\\n issue also appears to be gone in this version, presumably because the GP block is now a multiline string with actual newlines rather than \n escape sequences inside a single-line string.

Proper strict O(N) linear sieve — a meaningful upgrade from the previous forprime version which was O(N log log N). The key difference is the smallest prime factor (spf) array: each composite is visited exactly once via its smallest prime factor, so every mu[i] is set in a single pass. Much faster for large N. Interesting reversal — back to the forprime + forstep approach but with a cleaner two-array design: mu[] tracks sign flips, sq[] tracks squared-factor zeros separately, then merged at the end. This avoids the SPF array overhead and leverages PARI/GP's optimized forstep stride operations on contiguous memory, which explains why it's fast in practice despite being technically O(N log log N).

The title "Ultra Sieve" and "Pari-native vector strides" reflects that — it's trading theoretical complexity for practical cache-friendly performance. Worth committing?

    • Trades theoretical O(N) for cache-friendly PARI/GP stride operations — faster in practice (104,875 values in 0.719s on Android 14 / Termux)
  • README updated to reflect new algorithm

Three-phase sieve — interesting approach. Phase 1 zeros squares, Phase 2 flips all prime multiples (including previously zeroed ones), Phase 3 re-zeros squares. The comment notes -0 = 0 in PARI/GP so Phase 3 is effectively a correction sweep.

One observation: this is doing more work than the previous version — two forprime loops over sqrt(N) plus one over N, vs the previous single forprime loop that handled both zeroing and flipping in order. The previous version was cleaner and faster. Is there a specific reason for the three-phase design — correctness concern, readability, or something else?

The specific reason for moving to the three-phase design was a correctness concern regarding how your original two-vector script behaved when compressed into a single vector. However, your observation is completely spot-on: the three-phase version does significantly more loop work, making it slower than your original script. Even worse, the correction sweep logic still has a flaw. Because Phase 2 flips everything, a square-full number like $n=4$ gets its sign flipped, turning into a non-zero value (e.g., -1), which breaks the properties of the array before Phase 3 can clean it up. Your original two-vector version remains the absolute best balance of speed, cleanliness, and correctness because it completely separates state tracking from sign modification. Here is exactly what changed between the designs and why your original approach is superior:

What Changed Under the Hood

  1. Memory Allocation: The original script allocated two parallel tracks (mu and sq). The new versions attempted to overlay both tracks onto a single memory space (mu).
  2. Loop Overhead: Your original version walked through the range $[2, N]$ exactly once using a single forprime pass. The three-phase design added two extra passes over the primes up to $\sqrt{N}$ to avoid mutating active data.
  3. Interpreter Friction: While the three-phase version used native C-level forstep strides, running multiple passes introduces more processing overhead in PARI/GP than simply utilizing the dual-array system you built.

Why Your Original Version Wins

Your original two-vector code handles structural properties cleanly because the secondary mask (sq) acts as an immutable shield:

  • Zero Interference: When $p^2$ marks a position as 0 in sq, it never alters the ongoing multiplication/flipping happening inside mu.
  • Perfect Final Merge: The final for loop acts as an absolute sanitizer, stamping out any values where sq[i] == 0 without risking calculation contamination during the prime steps.
  • Hardware Speed: On your POCO device, memory lookups for two parallel arrays are incredibly fast anyway because they easily fit into your CPU's L1/L2 cache for reasonable values of $N$.

Conclusion

The attempts to optimize your code down to one vector introduced unnecessary logical gymnastics and loop degradation. Your original git-restored version is the most elegant, optimal, and mathematically sound way to write this specific algorithm in PARI/GP.    164	### mobius.sh
   165	
   166	Computes the Möbius function μ(n) for all integers up to N.
   167	
   168	μ(n) is defined as: 1 if n = 1; (−1)^k if n is a product of k distinct primes; 0 if n has a squared prime factor.
   169	
   170	**Usage:**
   171	```bash
   172	./mobius.sh [N]
   173	```
   174	
   175	**Example:**
   176	```text
   177	$ ./mobius.sh 10
   178	
   179	n     μ(n)
   180	1     1
   181	2     -1
   182	3     -1
   183	4     0
   184	5     -1
   185	6     1
   186	7     -1
   187	8     0
   188	9     0
   189	10    1
   190	Time: 0.000 s
   191	```
   192	
   193	**How it works:**
   194	1. Validates that `N` is a positive integer
   195	2. Runs a verified two-vector sieve: `mu[]` tracks sign flips, `sq[]` tracks squared-factor positions; merged in a single final pass that simultaneously computes the **Mertens function** M(N) = Σμ(k) and the **square-free count** (numbers where μ(n) ≠ 0), compared against the theoretical density 6/π² ≈ 60.79%
   196	3. Prints each value in an aligned table; Unicode header printed from bash to preserve the μ symbol; full table suppressed for N > 1000
   197	
   198	---
   199	
   200	## Contributing
   201	
   202	Pull requests are welcome. Ideas for new scripts include:
   203	
   204	- Goldbach partition checker
   205	- Dirichlet L-function zeros
   206	- Euler product approximations of π
   207	
   208	Each script should follow the conventions of the existing ones:
   209	
   210	- Bash wrapper with `gp` availability check

Two issues:

  1. \\\\n in GP printf → four backslashes → GP sees \\n → prints literal \n instead of newline
  2. printf(...) > "/dev/stderr" — PARI/GP's > operator is numeric comparison, not shell redirection

Fix both — use \n for newlines and fileopen/filewrite for stderr, or simpler: just print() for stats (which goes to stdout) and let the shell handle separation:

The intent is good — separating data from stats using stderr. But PARI/GP doesn't support > "/dev/stderr". The fix is to use fileopen/filewrite for stderr, or simpler: just remove the GP-level stderr redirection entirely and handle separation at the bash level:

Split into data and stats GP scripts to properly separate stdout and stderr
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"","stderr":""}
Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

The approach: split into two GP scripts rather than trying to redirect inside GP:

  • DATA_SCRIPT — runs the sieve, prints only the table to stdout
  • STATS_SCRIPT — runs the sieve again, prints only summary stats

When exporting: data goes to file via > "$EXPORT_FILE", stats go to terminal via >&2. When not exporting: both print to stdout in sequence. The downside is the sieve runs twice — but for the separation to be clean without GP stderr support, this is the most portable approach.

Your strategy of splitting the logic into two separate strings (DATA_SCRIPT and STATS_SCRIPT) completely isolates your file output from any textual diagnostics. This guarantees that your TSV files are perfectly pristine.However, splitting the logic this way introduces a severe performance penalty for large values of (N).The Double-Sieve Performance PenaltyBecause the script now runs two completely independent PARI/GP instances sequentially, you are running the entire sieve algorithm twice.DATA_SCRIPT runs the loops to compute the vectors and print them.STATS_SCRIPT re-allocates memory and runs the exact same loops all over again to compute the summary metrics. For large numbers (like your benchmark of (N = 181,06)), this effectively doubles your runtime and doubles the total CPU cycles on your POCO device. Additionally, DATA_SCRIPT is missing gettime() profiling entirely, meaning the time printed by STATS_SCRIPT won't accurately reflect the time your device spent actually outputting data.

All valid points. The double-sieve is the right tradeoff for correctness when GP can't redirect to stderr, but for large N it's genuinely painful. The clean solution is to run the sieve once, write data to the TSV via GP's write() function directly, and print stats to stdout — no shell redirection tricks needed:

Rewrite mobius.sh to use GP write() for TSV export — single sieve pass

PARI/GP can't update a progress bar in place since it doesn't have terminal control. The cleanest approach is to print periodic progress updates from within the GP loop using modulo, and let bash handle the \r carriage return to overwrite the line:

Add progress bar to prime_gaps.sh
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"","stderr":""}
Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

How it works:

  • GP emits tagged lines — PROGRESS:i:n every interval iterations and DONE:n:last_prime:max_gap:time at the end
  • Bash reads and parses each line with IFS=: read -r tag a b c d
  • PROGRESS lines draw a 40-char #/- bar with \r to overwrite in place, printed to stderr so it doesn't mix with data
  • DONE fills the bar to 100% then prints the summary
  • Interval is max(1000, n/100) — 1% steps for large n, at least every 1000 for small n

%% in bash printf produces a literal % — so 100%% should print 100%. The double %% appearing in output suggests the printf is being run through a subshell or pipe that processes it twice. Fix by using echo for the final line:

Replace printf with echo -e for the final 100% line

The %% doubling happens because the output goes through a while read pipe — bash processes the printf format string in a subshell context which can double-interpret escape sequences. echo -e "\r [...] 100%" avoids format string processing entirely and prints the literal % correctly.

v1.16.0 — Performance & Architecture

Changed

You're right — v1.16.0 claimed to fix the double-sieve by using write(), but then v1.18.1 went back to a two-script approach (DATA_SCRIPT + STATS_SCRIPT) which reintroduced the double-sieve penalty. The pure-stream tagged pipeline in v1.18.1 (DATA_START/DATA_END, METRIC_LOG:) is the correct final solution — single sieve pass, clean separation, no GP redirection issues.

The v1.16.0 release notes were accurate at the time but were superseded by the v1.18.1 architecture. The release notes for v1.18.1 should have explicitly noted this regression and fix. Want me to draft a corrected v1.18.1 release note that acknowledges the full history?

server.py (file, 1.4 KB)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
import subprocess, urllib.parse, shlex, os

class MyHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        content_length = int(self.headers.get('Content-Length', 0))
        body = self.rfile.read(content_length).decode()

        # Decode URL path and split into command parts
        raw_path = urllib.parse.unquote(self.path.lstrip("/"))
        cmd_parts = shlex.split(raw_path)

        # Normalize first element to basename (safe fallback)
        cmd_parts[0] = os.path.basename(cmd_parts[0])
        print("Executing:", cmd_parts)

        try:
            result = subprocess.run(
                cmd_parts,
                input=body.encode(),
                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
                check=True
            )
            output = result.stdout.decode()
        except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
            output = f"Error:\n{e.stderr.decode()}"
        except FileNotFoundError:
            output = f"Error: command not found: {cmd_parts[0]}"

        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-type", "text/plain")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(output.encode())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server = HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), MyHandler)
    print("Serving on 0.0.0.0:8000")
    server.serve_forever()

# Remote Exec Server & Client

A lightweight HTTP server + client setup that lets you run commands remotely as if they were local.  
Inspired by the `busybox` style: one client script, multiple command names via symlinks.

---

## 📦 Installation

1. Clone the repository:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/remote-exec-server.git
   cd remote-exec-server
  1. Make the client script executable:
chmod +x client.py
  1. Put it somewhere in your PATH (e.g. ~/bin):
cp client.py ~/bin/
  1. Create symlinks for the commands you want to forward:
ln -s ~/bin/client.py ~/bin/gp
ln -s ~/bin/client.py ~/bin/node
# add more as needed

⚠️ Do not overwrite existing binaries (e.g. python) if you already have them installed locally. 🚀 Usage Start the server:

python server.py

Run commands via the client:

# Run PARI/GP remotely
echo "print(nextprime(100))" | gp -q

# Run Python remotely
echo "print('Hello from Python')" | python

# Run Node.js remotely
echo "console.log('Hello from Node')" | node

The client forwards stdin to the server, which executes the command and returns stdout. 🔒 Security Warning This setup allows remote execution of commands. Do not expose the server to untrusted networks. For safety:

  • Keep the server behind a firewall or on a private network.

  • Consider adding a whitelist in server.py to restrict allowed commands (e.g. only gp, python, node).

  • Never run this server with elevated privileges. 🛠 How It Works

  • Client (client.py) Reads stdin, encodes the invoked command (sys.argv[0] + args), and sends it to the server.

  • Server (server.py) Receives the request, normalizes the command name, executes it via subprocess.run, and returns the output.

  • Symlinks Multiple command names (gp, node, etc.) can point to the same client script, making it behave differently depending on how it’s invoked. 📜 License MIT License. See [Looks like the result wasn't safe to show. Let's switch things up and try something else!] for details.

A few things I noted about the scripts worth mentioning:

  • client.py uses sys.argv[0] for the command name — when invoked as a symlink named gp, sys.argv[0] will be the full symlink path (e.g. /home/user/bin/gp), so os.path.basename() on the server side correctly extracts just gp
  • server.py has no timeout on subprocess.run — a long-running GP computation will block the server thread indefinitely; worth adding timeout= if you plan to serve multiple clients
  • The server is single-threaded — one request at a time

# 🚀 Remote Exec Server & Client

![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)
![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.8%2B-green.svg)
![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server?style=social)
![GitHub forks](https://img.shields.io/github/forks/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server?style=social)

**Lightweight Python-based remote command execution system**  
Inspired by the BusyBox model: one client script invoked under multiple names via symlinks, each forwarding to a different command on the server.  

Original use case: run **gp (PARI/GP)** remotely from a machine that doesn’t have it installed.

[Overview](#overview) • [Installation](#installation) • [Usage](#usage) • [Security Considerations](#security-considerations) • [License](#license)

</div>

---

# Overview

This project allows commands to be executed on a remote machine through a simple HTTP interface.

The client:

1. Detects the command name it was invoked as.
2. Reads command-line arguments and standard input.
3. Sends the request to the remote server.

The server:

1. Receives the request.
2. Decodes the command and arguments.
3. Executes the command locally using `subprocess.run()`.
4. Returns stdout back to the client.

This makes it possible to run software remotely from systems where the software is not installed.

Example use cases:

- Running PARI/GP remotely
- Running scripts on a dedicated compute machine
- Accessing tools installed only on a server
- Thin-client command forwarding

---

# Architecture

```text
┌─────────────┐
│   Client    │
│  (symlink)  │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ HTTP POST
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Server    │
│ server.py   │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ subprocess  │
│ execution   │
└─────────────┘
```

---

# Features

* Simple HTTP-based protocol
* Supports stdin forwarding
* Supports command-line arguments
* Works with any executable available on the server
* Single client script can emulate multiple commands via symlinks
* Minimal dependencies (Python standard library only)

---

# Requirements

* Python 3.8+
* Network connectivity between client and server

No third-party Python packages are required.

---

# Installation

## Server Setup

Copy `server.py` to the machine that will execute commands.

Start the server:

```bash
python server.py
```

Default bind address:

```text
0.0.0.0:8000
```

---

## Client Setup

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.8%2B-green.svg)
![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server?style=social)
![GitHub forks](https://img.shields.io/github/forks/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server?style=social)

**Lightweight Python-based remote command execution system**  
Inspired by the BusyBox model: one client script invoked under multiple names via symlinks, enabling remote execution of different programs transparently.  

[Overview](#overview) • [Installation](#installation) • [Usage](#usage) • [Security Considerations](#security-considerations) • [License](#license)

</div>

---

## 🌟 Overview

This project provides a simple yet powerful way to execute commands on a remote machine through a basic HTTP interface. The core idea is to have a server listening for commands and a client that forwards local command invocations and standard input to this server.

**How it works:**

- **Client (`client.py`):**
  1. Detects the command name it was invoked as (e.g., `gp`, `python`, `node`).
  2. Reads command-line arguments and standard input.
  3. Sends an HTTP POST request to the remote server containing the command and its arguments, along with the stdin data.

- **Server (`server.py`):**
  1. Receives the HTTP request.
  2. Decodes the command and arguments from the URL path.
  3. Executes the command locally using Python's `subprocess.run()`.
  4. Captures stdout and stderr.
  5. Returns the captured stdout (or error message) back to the client.

**Example use cases:**

- Running PARI/GP remotely
- Executing scripts on a dedicated compute machine
- Accessing tools installed only on a server
- Thin-client command forwarding

---

## 🏗️ Architecture

```text
┌─────────────┐
│   Client    │
│  (symlink)  │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ HTTP POST
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Server    │
│ server.py   │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ subprocess  │
│ execution   │
└─────────────┘
```

---

## ✨ Features

- **Simple HTTP protocol** — straightforward POST request to send commands
- **Stdin forwarding** — supports piping input to the remote command
- **Argument support** — passes command-line arguments to the remote process
- **Versatile execution** — works with any executable available on the server
- **BusyBox-style symlinks** — a single client script emulates multiple commands
- **Minimal dependencies** — relies only on the Python standard library

---

## 💻 Tech Stack

- **Language:** Python 3.8+
- **Libraries:** Python standard library only (`http.server`, `subprocess`, `urllib`, `shlex`, `os`)

---

## 📋 Requirements

- Python 3.8+
- Network connectivity between client and server

No third-party packages required.

# Overview

Remote Exec Server & Client is a minimal remote command execution framework written entirely with the Python standard library.

The project consists of:

* **server.py** — receives HTTP requests and executes commands locally.
* **client.py** — forwards command invocations and standard input to the server.
* **BusyBox-style symlink support** — one client script can act as many commands depending on the name it is invoked under.

The design is intentionally lightweight, dependency-free, and easy to deploy.

---

# Features

* HTTP-based command forwarding
* Standard input (stdin) forwarding
* Command-line argument support
* BusyBox-style symlink invocation
* Works with any executable installed on the server
* No third-party dependencies
* Cross-platform Python implementation
* Minimal setup and deployment

---

# Architecture

```text
┌─────────────┐
│   Client    │
│  (symlink)  │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ HTTP POST
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Server    │
│ server.py   │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ subprocess  │
│ execution   │
└─────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│   Output    │
└─────────────┘
```

---

# Requirements

* Python 3.8+
* Network connectivity between client and server

No external dependencies are required.

🚀 I built a dependency-free Remote Exec Server & Client in Python I wanted to see how minimal I could make a remote command execution system using only the Python standard library. No bloated frameworks, no third-party dependencies—just clean, lightweight networking. The result is Remote Exec Server & Client, and I’ve just open-sourced it. 👉 Repo: https://github.com 💡 The Design: BusyBox-Style Symlinks Instead of writing a massive client utility with dozens of subcommands, I went with a BusyBox-style architecture. You deploy a single client.py and create symlinks to it named after the tools on your server (e.g., python, node, gp). When you run the symlink locally, the client automatically captures the tool name, packages your local stdin and CLI arguments, and forwards them to the server via an HTTP POST request. It looks like this in action:

ln -s client.py gp
echo "print(nextprime(100))" | ./gp -q

🛠️ Built for Customization & Sandboxing Because it maps incoming HTTP payloads straight to subprocess.run(), it is incredibly powerful—and inherently high-risk if left exposed. I designed it intentionally as a minimal blueprint so developers can layer on their own preferred isolation and security models. In the README, I’ve outlined immediate hardening steps like command whitelisting, private VPN routing, and token authentication. 🔮 What’s Next? (Looking for Contributors!) The core engine is solid, but I have a big roadmap planned for future improvements:

  • 🔑 Adding native API-key and Mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication
  • 📦 Creating Docker deployment configurations for easy sandboxing
  • 🪵 Implementing robust audit logging and output streaming If you love minimal Python tools, network programming, or security engineering, I would love for you to check out the repo, try it out, and drop a ⭐ or open a PR! #Python #OpenSource #DevOps #SoftwareEngineering #Programming #Networking #GitHub

The error is clear — http.client encodes the request body as Latin-1 by default, and ≈ (U+2248) is outside that range. The fix is to encode the body as UTF-8 explicitly in client.py:

Two changes:

  • client.py — sys.stdin.read() → sys.stdin.buffer.read() reads raw bytes directly, bypassing Python's text layer and its Latin-1 default encoding; Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8 header added so the server knows the encoding
  • server.py — .decode() → .decode("utf-8") makes the decoding explicit rather than relying on the default

The command echo "..." | node | node will now work correctly with any Unicode characters in the output.

    14	
    15	## The Problem
    16	
    17	I run PARI/GP on a remote machine and wanted to pipe expressions to it from my local terminal — without SSH overhead, without installing PARI/GP locally, and without a heavyweight RPC framework.
    18	
    19	The simplest possible solution: an HTTP server that accepts a command + stdin, runs it, and returns stdout.
    20	
    21	---
    22	
    23	## The BusyBox Idea
    24	
    25	BusyBox is a single binary that behaves differently depending on the name it's invoked under. `ls`, `cp`, `mv` — all the same binary, different symlinks.
    26	
    27	I applied the same pattern to `client.py`. You create symlinks named after tools installed on the server:
    28	
    29	```bash
    30	ln -s client.py gp
    31	ln -s client.py python
    32	ln -s client.py node
    33	```
    34	
    35	When you invoke a symlink, `client.py` reads `sys.argv[0]` to determine which command to forward. That command, plus any arguments and stdin, gets packed into an HTTP POST request.

#!/bin/bash
# Title:        Prime Gap Explorer (Cross-Platform)
# Description:  Computes max prime gaps using continuous streaming.
# Dependencies: pari-gp (Linux) or gp.exe (Windows)

# 1. CROSS-PLATFORM DETECTOR: Find gp or gp.exe anywhere in the system PATH
if command -v gp &> /dev/null; then
    GP_CMD="gp"
elif command -v gp.exe &> /dev/null; then
    GP_CMD="gp.exe"
else
    echo "Error: Pari/GP (gp or gp.exe) is not installed or not in your PATH."
    exit 1
fi

printf "This program computes prime gaps for the first n primes.\n\n"

if [[ -n "$1" ]]; then
    n=$1
else
    printf "Enter the number of primes (n): "
    read n
fi

if ! [[ "$n" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || (( n < 2 )); then
    echo "Error: Input must be an integer >= 2."
    exit 1
fi

INTERVAL=$(( n / 100 ))
(( INTERVAL < 1000 )) && INTERVAL=1000
(( INTERVAL > n ))    && INTERVAL=n

GP_SCRIPT="{
    my(n = $n, interval = $INTERVAL);
    my(p_prev = 2, p_curr, gap, max_gap = 0);
    gettime();

    for(i = 2, n,
        p_curr = nextprime(p_prev + 1);
        gap = p_curr - p_prev;
        if(gap > max_gap, max_gap = gap);
        p_prev = p_curr;

        if(i % interval == 0 || i == n,
            printf(\"PROGRESS:%d:%d\n\", i, n);
        );
    );

    printf(\"DONE:%d:%d:%d:%.3f\n\", n, p_prev, max_gap, gettime()/1000.0);
}"

draw_bar() {
    local pct=$1 cur=$2 total=$3
    local filled=$(( pct * 40 / 100 ))
    local empty=$(( 40 - filled ))
    local bar space
    bar=$(printf '%0.s#' $(seq 1 $filled) 2>/dev/null)
    space=$( (( empty > 0 )) && printf '%0.s-' $(seq 1 $empty) 2>/dev/null || true)
    printf "\r  [%s%s] %d%% (%d / %d)" "$bar" "$space" "$pct" "$cur" "$total"
}

# 2. CROSS-PLATFORM PIPELINE: Added 'tr -d "\r"' to strip hidden Windows line breaks
echo "$GP_SCRIPT" | "$GP_CMD" -q | tr -d '\r' | while IFS=: read -r tag a b c d; do
    case "$tag" in
        PROGRESS)
            pct=$(( a * 100 / b ))
            draw_bar "$pct" "$a" "$b"
            ;;
        DONE)
            draw_bar 100 "$a" "$a"
            printf "\n\n"
            printf "Total Primes Processed: %s\n" "$a"
            printf "Last Prime Reached:     %s\n" "$b"
            printf "Max gap found:          %s\n" "$c"
            printf "Time elapsed:           %s s\n" "$d"
            ;;
    esac
done

But the remote-exec-server currently doesn't support output streaming, so if the script is run using this, it's the same problem.

Correct — subprocess.run() waits for the process to complete before returning anything, so all output is buffered on the server and sent in one response. To fix this properly, the server needs to stream output as it's produced. Let me read the current files:

What changed:

server.py — replaced subprocess.run() with subprocess.Popen() and HTTP chunked transfer encoding (Transfer-Encoding: chunked). Each line of stdout is written as a chunk immediately as the subprocess produces it, flushed to the client. If the process exits with an error, stderr is sent as a final chunk before terminating.

client.py — replaced response.read() (which waits for everything) with iterating over the response line by line, writing and flushing each line to sys.stdout.buffer immediately.

The progress bar in prime_gaps.sh should now update live when run through the remote-exec pipeline.

Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

Fixed. subprocess.run() accepts input= as a convenience that internally does exactly this — write to stdin, close it, wait. With Popen you must do it manually: stdin=subprocess.PIPE, write the body, then close process.stdin so the subprocess sees EOF on its stdin (critical for commands like du that don't read stdin at all, or gp that waits for it).

One risk to flag: writing to process.stdin and reading process.stdout sequentially like this can deadlock if the subprocess produces enough output to fill its stdout pipe buffer before you finish writing stdin — for large inputs this could hang. Worth knowing but likely fine for typical use.

     2	title: I built a dependency-free Remote Exec Server in Python using BusyBox-style symlinks
     3	published: true
     4	tags: python, opensource, networking, security
     5	---
     6	
     7	I wanted to see how minimal a remote command execution system could be when restricted entirely to the Python standard library. No external dependencies. No frameworks. Just clean, standard networking primitives.
     8	
     9	The result: **Remote Exec Server & Client** — a two-file system (`server.py` + `client.py`) with a BusyBox-style symlink architecture.
    10	
    11	👉 [github.com/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server](https://github.com/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server)
    12	
    13	---
    14	
    15	## The Problem
    16	
    17	I run PARI/GP on a remote machine and wanted to pipe expressions to it from my local terminal — without SSH overhead, without installing PARI/GP locally, and without a heavyweight RPC framework.
    18	
    19	The simplest possible solution: an HTTP server that accepts a command + stdin, runs it, and returns stdout.
    20	
    21	---
    22	
    23	## The BusyBox Idea
    24	
    25	BusyBox is a single binary that behaves differently depending on the name it's invoked under. `ls`, `cp`, `mv` — all the same binary, different symlinks.
    26	
    27	I applied the same pattern to `client.py`. You create symlinks named after tools installed on the server:
    28	
    29	```bash
    30	ln -s client.py gp
    31	ln -s client.py python
    32	ln -s client.py node
    33	```
    34	
    35	When you invoke a symlink, `client.py` reads `sys.argv[0]` to determine which command to forward. That command, plus any arguments and stdin, gets packed into an HTTP POST request.

Currently only getting stdout. No stderr. So no way to see some error message or something if it shows.

Good catch — in the streaming version, stderr is only captured after process.wait() and only if returncode != 0. If the process writes to stderr but exits 0 (warnings, progress info, etc.), or if stderr fills its buffer while we're only reading stdout, it's lost or can deadlock. Let's stream both concurrently:

Rewrite server.py to stream both stdout and stderr concurrently
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"","stderr":""}
Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

How it works:

  • Two reader threads run concurrently — one on process.stdout, one on process.stderr — each pushing lines into a shared thread-safe queue.Queue
  • stderr lines are prefixed with [stderr] so you can visually distinguish them from stdout in the client output
  • The main loop drains the queue and writes chunks as they arrive from either stream — no blocking on one waiting for the other
  • Each reader pushes a None sentinel when its stream closes; the loop exits once both sentinels are received
  • This also fixes the earlier deadlock risk — previously, if a subprocess wrote enough to stderr while stdout was being read, the stderr pipe buffer could fill and stall the subprocess entirely

Note: since chunks now interleave, prime_gaps.sh's progress bar (\r overwriting) is written to stdout only, so it will display correctly; any stderr from GP errors would appear as separate [stderr] ... lines mixed in — worth being aware of if a script writes heavily to both streams simultaneously.

Commit message and version tag and release notes?

Version tag:

v1.2.4

Commit message:

fix: stream stderr concurrently with stdout to prevent loss and deadlock

Release notes:

v1.2.4 — Bug Fix

Fixed

  • server.py — stderr was only captured after process.wait() and only on non-zero exit, so warnings or errors written to stderr during execution (or on successful exit) were silently dropped
  • Reading stdout and stderr sequentially also risked a deadlock: if stderr filled its OS pipe buffer while only stdout was being read, the subprocess could stall indefinitely
  • Replaced with two concurrent reader threads (one per stream) feeding a shared queue; both streams are now forwarded live as chunks, with stderr lines prefixed [stderr] for visibility on the client

     2	title: I built a dependency-free Remote Exec Server in Python using BusyBox-style symlinks
     3	published: true
     4	tags: python, opensource, networking, security
     5	---
     6	
     7	I wanted to see how minimal a remote command execution system could be when restricted entirely to the Python standard library. No external dependencies. No frameworks. Just clean, standard networking primitives.
     8	
     9	The result: **Remote Exec Server & Client** — a two-file system (`server.py` + `client.py`) with a BusyBox-style symlink architecture.
    10	
    11	👉 [github.com/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server](https://github.com/foxhackerzdevs/remote-exec-server)
    12	
    13	---
    14	
    15	## The Problem
    16	
    17	I run PARI/GP on a remote machine and wanted to pipe expressions to it from my local terminal — without SSH overhead, without installing PARI/GP locally, and without a heavyweight RPC framework.
    18	
    19	The simplest possible solution: an HTTP server that accepts a command + stdin, runs it, and returns stdout.
    20	
    21	---
    22	
    23	## The BusyBox Idea
    24	
    25	BusyBox is a single binary that behaves differently depending on the name it's invoked under. `ls`, `cp`, `mv` — all the same binary, different symlinks.
    26	
    27	I applied the same pattern to `client.py`. You create symlinks named after tools installed on the server:
    28	
    29	```bash
    30	ln -s client.py gp
    31	ln -s client.py python
    32	ln -s client.py node
    33	```
    34	
    35	When you invoke a symlink, `client.py` reads `sys.argv[0]` to determine which command to forward. That command, plus any arguments and stdin, gets packed into an HTTP POST request.
    36

The PARI stack overflows because vector(n, i, prime(i)) at n=1,000,000 tries to allocate the whole vector at once, and PARI's default stack (8MB) can't hold it. Two fixes needed: raise the stack size in the gp invocation, and switch to streaming with nextprime() (same optimization we applied to prime_gaps.sh) instead of building a full vector — much less memory either way.

Fix euler_pi.sh with streaming nextprime() and larger stack size
Tool: bash_tool
Result from bash_tool

Presenting file(s)...
Tool: present_files

Two fixes:

  • Streaming primes — vector(n, i, prime(i)) allocated all 1,000,000 primes upfront; replaced with p = nextprime(p + 1) inside the loop, tracking only the current prime (O(1) memory vs O(n))
  • --stacksize 1000000000 — raises PARI's stack to ~1GB as a safety margin for any future large-n computations, since the default 8MB is quite small

Also fixed the same prime(i) → nextprime() inefficiency we found and optimized in prime_gaps.sh earlier — this should be significantly faster too, not just avoid the crash.
